I have been thinking about the strange freedom of walking without a destination. Most of our movement is purposeful—errands, commutes, obligations. But when I leave the house with no map, no schedule, something in my mind loosens. Streets become suggestions rather than routes. I notice the way a sycamore leans into the wind, the particular blue of a door I have passed a hundred times.

This aimlessness feels, paradoxically, like a form of attention. Without the pressure to arrive, I can finally be where I am. The city unfolds as texture: a cat sleeping in a window, the smell of bread from a basement vent, the distant clatter of a train. These small details are always there, but purpose narrows vision. Walking without destination widens it.

I suspect this is true of writing as well. When I sit down with a rigid plan, I often produce something brittle. When I allow the first sentence to wander, the next one finds its own way. Meaning emerges not from forcing direction but from following curiosity.

Perhaps we need more sanctioned uselessness—more time spent not optimizing, not achieving, not knowing exactly where we are going. I used to feel guilty about this, as if idleness were a debt to be repaid. I no longer think that way. There is a kind of intelligence in drifting. It reminds us that not every path must lead somewhere. Some paths are just for the walking. The walk itself is the destination. That is enough.
